title: How is a load balancer implemented in Azure (Azure Load Balancer L4, Application Gateway L7, Front Door global, AKS LoadBalancer service)?
shortTitle: How is a load balancer implemented in Azure

s1_definition.profdef: Azure provides a layered set of load-balancing services for different scopes and OSI layers. Azure Load Balancer is a regional layer-four balancer that distributes TCP and UDP traffic across backend instances by connection, with no awareness of HTTP. Application Gateway is a regional layer-seven balancer that understands HTTP, enabling path-based and host-based routing, TLS termination, and a Web Application Firewall. Azure Front Door is a global layer-seven service that routes users to the nearest healthy region over Microsoft's edge network with global failover and caching. In Azure Kubernetes Service, creating a Service of type LoadBalancer automatically provisions an Azure Load Balancer and wires it to the healthy Pods. You combine them, for example Front Door globally in front of regional Application Gateways in front of AKS.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants to route customers efficiently. Azure Load Balancer is the doorman inside one branch who simply sends each arriving customer to whichever counter is free, counting heads but not reading their forms, which is fast and simple. Application Gateway is a smarter concierge in that same branch who actually reads the request on the form and sends loan questions to the loans desk and deposit questions to the deposits desk, and who also checks each visitor for trouble at the door, which is the firewall. Azure Front Door is the national call-routing center that, when a customer calls the toll-free number from anywhere in the country, connects them to the nearest healthy branch and instantly reroutes to another city if one branch is down. In Azure Kubernetes Service, asking for a LoadBalancer service is like telling the building management "give me a doorman," and they automatically install and wire one up for you.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Azure provides a layered set of load-balancing services for different scopes and OSI layers. Azure Load Balancer is a regional layer-four balancer that distributes TCP and UDP traffic across backend instances by connection, with no awareness of HTTP. Application Gateway is a regional layer-seven balancer that understands HTTP, enabling path-based and host-based routing, TLS termination, and a Web Application Firewall. Azure Front Door is a global layer-seven service that routes users to the nearest healthy region over Microsoft's edge network with global failover and caching. In Azure Kubernetes Service, creating a Service of type LoadBalancer automatically provisions an Azure Load Balancer and wires it to the healthy Pods. You combine them, for example Front Door globally in front of regional Application Gateways in front of AKS.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants to route customers efficiently. Azure Load Balancer is the doorman inside one branch who simply sends each arriving customer to whichever counter is free, counting heads but not reading their forms, which is fast and simple. Application Gateway is a smarter concierge in that same branch who actually reads the request on the form and sends loan questions to the loans desk and deposit questions to the deposits desk, and who also checks each visitor for trouble at the door, which is the firewall. Azure Front Door is the national call-routing center that, when a customer calls the toll-free number from anywhere in the country, connects them to the nearest healthy branch and instantly reroutes to another city if one branch is down. In Azure Kubernetes Service, asking for a LoadBalancer service is like telling the building management "give me a doorman," and they automatically install and wire one up for you.

**One line to remember:** Azure layers its load balancers by scope and OSI layer — Load Balancer is regional L4, Application Gateway is regional L7 with a firewall, Front Door is global L7 with edge routing and failover, and AKS auto-provisions an Azure Load Balancer for a LoadBalancer-type Service.

sections.s2_technical:
Azure Load Balancer operates at layer four, meaning it balances TCP and UDP connections based on IP address and port without inspecting the content of the traffic. It distributes incoming flows across a backend pool of virtual machines or scale-set instances using hashing, typically a five-tuple hash of source and destination IP, port, and protocol, and it uses health probes to keep only healthy backends in the pool. It comes in public and internal flavors, where a public Load Balancer has a public IP for internet-facing traffic and an internal one balances within a virtual network. Its strengths are very high throughput, low latency, and simplicity, because it does not parse application data. Its limitation is exactly that it is layer four, so it cannot route by URL path or host, cannot terminate TLS, and cannot apply HTTP-aware rules. You use it when you need fast, protocol-agnostic balancing, for example in front of a set of virtual machines or as the data-plane balancer under AKS.

Application Gateway operates at layer seven, understanding HTTP and HTTPS, which unlocks application-aware features. It supports path-based routing, so requests to `/api/v1/transfers` go to one backend pool and `/api/v1/loans` to another, and host-based routing by the requested hostname. It terminates TLS at the gateway, offloading encryption from the backends, and it supports cookie-based session affinity, URL rewriting, and autoscaling. A major feature is the integrated Web Application Firewall, which inspects requests for common attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting and blocks them before they reach the application, which matters a great deal for a bank. It is regional, meaning it serves one Azure region. You use it when you need HTTP-aware routing, TLS offload, and a firewall in front of regional web applications.

Azure Front Door is the global layer-seven entry point. It uses Microsoft's worldwide edge network to accept user traffic at the nearest point of presence and route it to the closest healthy backend region, which reduces latency through anycast and split-TCP optimizations. It provides global server load balancing with automatic failover, so if an entire region becomes unhealthy, Front Door routes users to another region. It also offers edge caching for static content, TLS termination at the edge, and its own Web Application Firewall at the global tier. Because it is global, it is what you place at the very front of a multi-region deployment, and it complements rather than replaces the regional balancers behind it. You use Front Door when you serve users across geographies and need global routing, low latency, and resilience to a whole-region outage.

In Azure Kubernetes Service, load balancing is largely automatic through Kubernetes primitives mapped to Azure resources. When you create a Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer, the Azure cloud controller automatically provisions an Azure Load Balancer, assigns it a public or internal IP, and configures its backend pool and health probes to target the Service's healthy Pod endpoints, so external traffic reaching that IP is distributed to the Pods. For layer-seven routing inside AKS you typically add an ingress controller, such as the Application Gateway Ingress Controller, which programs an Application Gateway from Kubernetes Ingress resources, or an in-cluster ingress like NGINX fronted by an Azure Load Balancer. The senior-level framing is that these services compose into a tiered architecture: Front Door globally distributes and fails over across regions, each region's Application Gateway does HTTP routing, TLS termination, and firewalling, an Azure Load Balancer provides the fast layer-four data plane, and inside AKS the LoadBalancer Service and ingress controller connect all of this to the Pods, with health probes at every tier ensuring traffic only ever reaches healthy targets. You choose the combination based on whether you need global reach, HTTP awareness, a firewall, and Kubernetes integration.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India runs its transfer platform on Azure, serving customers across the country, with workloads in two regions on AKS.

Problem 1 — initially everything sat behind a single regional layer-four Azure Load Balancer, which spread connections fine but could not route `/api/v1/transfers` and `/api/v1/loans` to different backend pools and could not inspect requests for attacks. This is exactly the limitation of layer four, and it motivates Application Gateway at layer seven for path-based routing, TLS termination, and the Web Application Firewall.

Problem 2 — customers far from the single region experienced high latency, and when that region had an outage, the whole platform went down. This is exactly what Azure Front Door solves: global edge routing to the nearest healthy region and automatic failover to the other region on a regional outage.

Problem 3 — the team ran the services on AKS and needed external traffic to reach the Pods without manually wiring IPs and probes. This is exactly what a Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer provides: Azure auto-provisions a Load Balancer wired to the healthy Pods.

The mini-project models these Azure tiers in code to make the routing decisions explicit: an `AzureLoadBalancerL4` that picks a backend by five-tuple-style hashing, an `ApplicationGatewayL7` that routes by path and runs a simple WAF check, a `FrontDoorGlobal` that selects the nearest healthy region and fails over, and an `AksLoadBalancerService` that represents auto-provisioned Pod backends. The demo sends requests from different regions and paths, shows Front Door choosing a region and failing over, Application Gateway routing by path and blocking a malicious request, and the layer-four balancer distributing to Pods.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the Azure load-balancing tiers demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.azurelb.AzureLbDemo

# Provision real Azure resources with Bicep / CLI
az deployment group create -g nbi-rg --template-file bicep/main.bicep

# AKS: creating a LoadBalancer Service auto-provisions an Azure Load Balancer
kubectl apply -f service.yaml
kubectl get service transfer-service      # EXTERNAL-IP assigned by Azure LB

# Inspect the tiers
az network front-door show -n nbi-frontdoor -g nbi-rg
az network application-gateway show -n nbi-appgw-south -g nbi-rg
az network lb show -n nbi-lb-south -g nbi-rg
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a user whose latency is twenty milliseconds to the centralindia region and ninety to southeastasia, an AKS Pod pool with one Pod marked down, and three requests: a transfer, a loan, and a malicious injection attempt, followed by a regional outage.

Step 1: The request arrives at Azure Front Door, the global tier. Front Door compares the healthy regions by latency from the user and picks centralindia at twenty milliseconds as the nearest healthy region. This is global edge routing in action.

Step 2: Within centralindia, the AKS Service of type LoadBalancer has already auto-provisioned an Azure Load Balancer wired to the Pod endpoints, and its readiness-based pool excludes the Pod marked down, so only the two healthy transfer Pods are eligible.

Step 3: The transfer request reaches the regional Application Gateway at layer seven. It inspects the path, sees it begins with the transfers prefix, and routes to the transfer backend pool, then the layer-four data plane picks a specific Pod by connection hash. The response flows back through the terminated TLS connection.

Step 4: The loan request similarly reaches Application Gateway, which routes it by path to the loan pool instead, demonstrating path-based routing that the layer-four balancer alone could not do.

Step 5: The malicious request arrives with a SQL-injection payload. The Application Gateway's Web Application Firewall inspects it, matches the injection pattern, and blocks it with a 403 before it ever reaches a Pod, which is exactly why a layer-seven gateway with a firewall matters for a bank.

Step 6: The centralindia region then goes unhealthy. Front Door's health checks detect this, and on the next request it selects southeastasia as the only remaining healthy region, failing over automatically. The user is now served from the other region with no manual intervention, demonstrating global failover.

```
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    FRONT DOOR route to nearest healthy region: centralindia (20ms)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    AKS Service type=LoadBalancer -> Azure LB auto-provisioned for 3 pods
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    APPGW L7 path /api/v1/transfers -> pool transfer
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    transfer request served by pod: 10.1.0.12
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    APPGW L7 path /api/v1/loans -> pool loan
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    loan request served by pod: 10.1.1.22
2026-10-24 12:45:00 SEVERE  WAF BLOCK malicious request: name=' OR '1'='1

2026-10-24 12:45:00 SEVERE  centralindia region is now UNHEALTHY
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    FRONT DOOR route to nearest healthy region: southeastasia (90ms)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Azure provides a layered set of load-balancing services, and the way I keep them straight is by scope and OSI layer. Azure Load Balancer is a regional layer-four service that distributes TCP and UDP traffic across a backend pool using a five-tuple hash, with health probes keeping only healthy backends in rotation. It is extremely fast and simple because it does not inspect application content, but that is also its limit: it cannot route by URL path or host, cannot terminate TLS, and cannot apply HTTP-aware rules. I use it when I need fast protocol-agnostic balancing, for example in front of virtual machines or as the data-plane balancer under AKS.

Application Gateway is a regional layer-seven service that understands HTTP, which unlocks path-based and host-based routing, so requests to the transfers path go to one backend pool and the loans path to another, plus TLS termination to offload encryption from the backends, session affinity, and URL rewriting. Crucially for a bank, it includes an integrated Web Application Firewall that inspects requests for attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting and blocks them before they reach the application. I use it when I need HTTP-aware routing, TLS offload, and a firewall in front of regional web apps.

Azure Front Door is the global layer-seven entry point. It uses Microsoft's worldwide edge network to accept traffic at the nearest point of presence and route it to the closest healthy backend region with anycast, which cuts latency, and it does global server load balancing with automatic failover, so if an entire region goes unhealthy it reroutes users to another region. It also offers edge caching, TLS at the edge, and a global-tier firewall. I put Front Door at the very front of a multi-region deployment, and it complements rather than replaces the regional balancers behind it.

In Azure Kubernetes Service the load balancing is largely automatic. When I create a Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer, the Azure cloud controller automatically provisions an Azure Load Balancer, assigns it a public or internal IP, and wires its backend pool and health probes to the Service's healthy Pod endpoints, so I never manually manage IPs or probes. For layer-seven routing inside AKS I add an ingress controller, often the Application Gateway Ingress Controller, which programs an Application Gateway from Kubernetes Ingress resources.

The way I frame it for an interviewer is that these services compose into a tiered architecture rather than competing: Azure Front Door globally distributes traffic and fails over across regions, each region's Application Gateway does HTTP routing, TLS termination, and firewalling, an Azure Load Balancer provides the fast layer-four data plane, and inside AKS a LoadBalancer-type Service plus an ingress controller connects all of that to the Pods, with health probes at every tier ensuring traffic only reaches healthy targets. On our banking platform we ran exactly this: Front Door in front of two regions, each with an Application Gateway doing path routing and WAF in front of an Azure Load Balancer and AKS, which gave us global low latency, regional failover, HTTP-aware routing, and attack protection all at once. I choose which tiers to use based on whether I need global reach, HTTP awareness, a firewall, and Kubernetes integration.

keyPoints: Horizontal scaling: add more instances behind load balancer
Vertical scaling: bigger machine — has limits
Auto-scaling: based on CPU, memory, request rate metrics
Sharding: partition data across databases for write scalability
